title: Race a hoop and a cylinder
materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: gentle book ramp, two sturdy round objects, clear desk; adult helps secure the ramp.
question: Does equal mass mean an equal finish time?
encounter: Before touching the controls, predict which wins: a hoop or a solid cylinder of equal mass and radius. Move the mass inward and watch the race again.
procedure: Choose two round objects and a gentle ramp over a clear desk, or use the model. Release together without a push.
Keep the ramp and starting height fixed. Compare finish times; repeat three times.
In the model, vary the inertia factor while leaving mass and radius fixed. Record model readings separately from physical observations.
explanation: Mass farther from the axis needs more energy for the same spin rate. Less of the height loss becomes forward kinetic energy.
limits: Rigid objects, no slipping, constant slope and negligible rolling resistance. The bodies are equal in mass and radius. Household containers may have moving contents; that needs a different model.
derivation: The height loss gives energy mgh (m in kg, g in m/s², h in m).
Rolling shares it: mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω². I is rotational inertia in kg·m².
No slip gives v = Rω. Write I = k mR², where k describes mass distribution.
Then v² = 2gh/(1+k) and a = g sin(θ)/(1+k).
worked: On a 30° ramp, a solid cylinder (k = 0.5) accelerates at 3.27 m/s²; a hoop (k = 1) at 2.45 m/s².
challenge: If you move the same mass towards the axis, which object now wins? Explain without calculating.

title: Balance is more than equal forces
materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: ruler, stable desk support, tiny known loads; no heavy balancing objects.
question: Can forces balance while the object starts turning?
encounter: Imagine pushing a door near the hinge, then near the handle with the same force. Which push turns it more easily?
procedure: Balance a ruler across a stable narrow support on a desk; keep loads small and off feet. Or use the beam model.
Put loads on opposite sides. Keep one position fixed and find a position that balances.
Repeat with a different pivot. Record distance from pivot, not distance from the ruler end.
explanation: A balanced beam needs zero net force and zero net torque. The separate free-bar force pair shows how zero net force can coexist with a turning effect.
limits: Beam: massless rigid beam with two point loads on a fixed frictionless pivot, shown horizontal at release. An unbalanced beam has angular acceleration and a downward centre-of-mass acceleration; the support reaction is calculated from both. Pair mode: view from above of a free bar; equal opposite in-plane forces, no pivot.
derivation: A downward load produces torque τ=−mg(x−p), in N·m, about pivot p. Counterclockwise is positive.
At balance, both torques cancel and the support equals total weight.
At release when unbalanced, Iα=Στ and the centre accelerates vertically: a_y=α(x_CM−p). The support is Mg+Ma_y, not generally Mg.
The separate free-bar example has equal opposite forces 0.4 m apart. Net force is zero but torque is −2×0.4=−0.8 N·m.
worked: A 0.2 kg load 0.2 m left balances 0.4 kg placed 0.1 m right of the pivot: both turning effects are 0.392 N·m.
challenge: Could two equal weights fail to balance? Give a placement and explain it.

observations.sampleNote: Illustrative balanced cases: pivot0, left .2 kg at −.2 m

title: Measure what a bounce returns
materials: Soft ball, ruler, clear floor and optional local slow-motion clip. Supplied observations need no equipment.
question: If 80% of the speed returns, does 80% of the energy return?
encounter: Press Play to watch the bounces. Then lower “Speed ratio e”, the fraction of speed kept after each bounce. Before playing again, guess whether the next bounce will be higher or lower.
procedure: Use the linked local video tracker to mark the highest point after each bounce; put a ruler in the same plane. Or use the supplied observations.
Keep ball, surface and camera position fixed. Enter successive drop and rebound heights in metres; repeat a height three times.
Compare your height ratios with the model. Explain where mechanical energy went and what measurement could test your account.
explanation: Height measures gravitational energy. Speed depends on the square root of height; speed ratio and energy ratio therefore differ.
limits: Vertical bounce from rest on a fixed floor, negligible air drag and rotation. Restitution is a ball/surface/impact-condition property, not a universal constant. Microphone echoes are not used as measurements.
derivation: Just before contact, ½mu² = mgH. After contact, ½mv² = mgh.
Restitution e = v/u = √(h/H). H and h are positive heights in the same unit.
Returned mechanical-energy fraction is h/H = e².
Ball-only momentum changes during contact because the floor exerts an external impulse. Total energy includes the floor and air.
worked: From 1.00 m to 0.64 m: e = 0.80 and mechanical-energy fraction = 0.64; 36% became other stores and sound.
challenge: A ball returns to half its height. Is its speed ratio one half? Explain.

observations.sampleNote: Illustrative observations; same ball and surface

title: Make a sealed diver sink
materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: sealed flexible packet, water and plastic bottle; adult helps choose a barely floating packet.
question: What changes when a sealed packet sinks after a squeeze?
encounter: A sealed flexible packet barely floats in water. Predict whether squeezing the bottle changes its mass, its volume, or both.
procedure: Use the supplied packet model, or with an adult select a sealed condiment packet that barely floats inside a plastic water bottle.
Squeeze gently, release, and describe the change before explaining it. Keep the packet sealed.
Compare air-pocket volume and displaced water at several pressures. This model uses fixed packet mass, not water entering an open diver.
explanation: The air compresses, making the sealed packet smaller. The packet displaces less water, so buoyancy can drop below its unchanged weight.
limits: Illustrative sealed packet: 9 mL incompressible material plus 1 mL air at 101.325 kPa, mass 9.8 g. Slow, approximately isothermal compression; water compression is neglected. A real packet may be too dense to float.
derivation: At fixed temperature and gas amount, P V_air is constant; pressure P must be absolute.
Total packet volume = 9 mL + compressed air volume. Mass remains 9.8 g.
Buoyancy = water density × g × displaced volume; water density is about 1000 kg/m³.
At a smaller packet volume, buoyancy can be less than weight. Sinking is a result of that force imbalance.
worked: Doubling pressure halves the 1 mL air pocket. Packet volume becomes 9.5 mL, below the 9.8 mL needed to support 9.8 g.
challenge: Would squeezing a completely solid incompressible packet work the same way? Why?

observations.sampleNote: Ideal model: fixed temperature, initial air1 mL

title: Warm it or squeeze it?
materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
question: Can two different changes produce the same pressure?
encounter: Predict the pressure when a fixed amount of gas is squeezed to half its volume. Then restore the volume and double its absolute temperature.
procedure: Choose the constant-temperature route and vary volume.
Choose the fixed-volume route and vary temperature in kelvin. Record the pressure each time.
Compare both with the baseline. Keep the amount of gas fixed; no heated sealed container is needed.
explanation: Gas pressure depends on amount, volume and absolute temperature. Compression and warming are different changes that can produce the same pressure ratio.
limits: Fixed gas amount, ideal gas, equilibrium states. Baseline: 1 L at 300 K and 101325 Pa. No real container heating or molecular collision trajectories are simulated.
derivation: The ideal gas relationship is PV = nRT; P in Pa, V in m³ and T in K.
For fixed n, P/P₀ = (T/T₀)(V₀/V).
At fixed T, halving V doubles P. At fixed V, doubling T doubles P.
A temperature ratio uses kelvin: doubling degrees Celsius is not doubling absolute temperature.
worked: 1 L at 600 K and 0.5 L at 300 K both give 202650 Pa for this fixed amount.
challenge: Does warming from 20°C to 40°C double pressure in a rigid container? Explain.

observations.sampleNote: Ideal model: fixed amount at300 K

title: One yo-yo, two questions
materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
question: Does a smaller axle make an unwinding yo-yo fall faster?
encounter: First imagine a yo-yo hanging without unwinding as a small-angle pendulum. Then let its string unwind. Are these the same model?
procedure: Use Pendulum to vary string length and predict the period.
Use Unwinding to compare axle radii while outer radius and mass distribution stay fixed.
Trace the same height loss into translation and rotation; record a model reading and explain why the pendulum formula no longer applies.
explanation: Unwinding couples the fall to spin through string tension. A small axle requires more spin for the same downward speed.
limits: Pendulum: point-bob approximation, small angle, no unwinding. Unwinding: fixed end, massless string, no slip on axle, no return tug, outer radius 4 cm and mass 1 kg. Illustrated angle is slowed.
derivation: For the pendulum, T = 2π√(L/g); bob mass cancels.
For unwinding, mg−tension = ma and tension × r = Iα.
No slip at the axle gives a = rα, hence a = g/(1+I/(mr²)).
With outer radius R and I = k mR², reduce axle r and more energy goes into rotation.
worked: For k=0.5, R=4 cm and r=1 cm, a=g/9≈1.09 m/s². This is not free fall.
challenge: Why does the same yo-yo need different equations when it hangs and when it unwinds?

observations.sampleNote: Ideal unwinding model: R4 cm, inertia factor.5

title: Calibrate a spring; question a rubber band
materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: small spring, ruler and tiny known loads over a desk; adult helps secure it.
question: Must every stretch graph be a straight line?
encounter: Predict whether doubling the load doubles the stretch. Compare an ideal spring with a stiffening rubber-like material.
procedure: Use a small spring and tiny known loads over a desk, or use the supplied observations. Mark the unloaded position.
Add loads gently and record extension, not total length. Repeat each load; hold the spring and ruler fixed.
Plot force against extension. Compare a straight-line model with the curved model. Real rubber may also show different loading and unloading paths.
explanation: A straight load–extension graph describes an approximately linear spring. Elastic recovery alone does not require a straight graph.
limits: Quasistatic loading; linear F=kx or illustrative nonlinear F=kx+800x³ (SI). The rubber-like curve is not a fit to a particular band and has no hysteresis. Do not stretch bands near eyes.
derivation: For a linear spring, force F=kx; stiffness k is in N/m.
Stored energy is the area under the force–extension graph.
For F=kx, that triangle has area ½kx² joules.
The nonlinear illustration adds 800x³ to force and 200x⁴ to energy. Real materials require measurements.
worked: A 20 N/m linear spring stretches 0.10 m under 2 N, storing 0.10 J.
challenge: If a rubber band springs back, must its graph be a straight line? What would you measure?

title: Why a spinning top precesses
materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
question: Does spin remove the downward force of gravity?
encounter: Predict what happens to the rate of precession if spin doubles while tilt stays the same. Keep the gravity arrow in view.
procedure: Choose a tilt and spin rate in the virtual top.
Follow the angular momentum arrow and the horizontal torque that turns it.
Record precession at several spin rates and compare the inverse trend. This is a steady-precession approximation, not a full top falling to rest.
explanation: Gravity still acts. Its torque changes the direction of angular momentum, so the axis sweeps around.
limits: Fast symmetric top, slow steady precession, fixed tilt; ignores nutation and spin loss. m=0.1 kg, centre 0.04 m from support, I=0.0001 kg·m². Spin 80–160 rad/s; precession is much slower. No physical balancing required. Torque projection is drawn about the support; the centre is not the pivot.
derivation: Spin angular momentum L≈Iω, in kg·m²/s.
Gravity produces torque magnitude mgℓ sinθ, in N·m.
A slowly precessing L sweeps at rate Ω, giving |dL/dt|≈ΩL sinθ.
Equate them: Ω≈mgℓ/(Iω). Doubling spin halves this precession rate.
worked: At ω=80 rad/s, Ω≈4.9 rad/s. At 160 rad/s it is≈2.45 rad/s.
challenge: Which force disappeared when the top began to spin? If none, what changed?

title: A flying disc needs more than a parabola
materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
question: What does a gravity-only prediction leave out?
encounter: Predict a disc trajectory first with gravity only. Switch on the simple aerodynamic model and compare the paths.
procedure: Choose the same launch speed and elevation for both models.
Compare range and flight time; record the model used beside every reading.
Explain which observations would need a better model: wind, changing angle of attack, wobble or spin loss. Use the virtual route indoors.
explanation: Moving air produces lift normal to the flight velocity and drag opposite it in this simplified model. Spin helps orientation stability but does not supply forward energy.
limits: Two-dimensional illustrative flight from 1 m, mass 0.175 kg, area 0.057 m², density 1.2 kg/m³, fixed C_L=.30 and C_D=.12. No attitude, spin or stall dynamics; launch elevation is not angle of attack. This is not a prediction for a particular disc.
derivation: Gravity-only motion has x=v₀ cosθ t and y=h+v₀ sinθ t−½gt².
Simple air forces have magnitudes L=½ρAv²C_L and D=½ρAv²C_D.
Here lift is perpendicular to velocity and drag opposes it; numerical integration follows their changing directions.
A real disc needs changing aerodynamic coefficients and attitude dynamics; equal transit time is not a valid explanation of lift.
worked: At 10 m/s and 30° from 1 m above the floor, the gravity-only range is about 10.32 m.
challenge: Can a decorative spinning disc on a parabolic path demonstrate lift? Explain what is missing.

observations.sampleNote: Gravity-only model;30° elevation; release height1 m

title: Shake, store, shine
materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
question: Can a stationary magnet keep a flashlight lit?
encounter: Set magnet speed to zero. Predict the generated voltage, then compare it with a moving magnet and stored charge.
procedure: Choose a representative magnet speed and a charging duration.
Stop shaking and increase the time since stopping. Watch the capacitor discharge into the lamp-equivalent load.
Record energy values and check the complete account, including winding heat. Compare with the linked generator.
explanation: Changing flux induces voltage. Hand work can become stored electrical energy, light and heat; taking energy out opposes the driving motion.
limits: Ideal rectified source E=2v, a 0.1 F capacitor charged through 10Ω, then discharged through a 10Ω lamp-equivalent. No LED threshold, real magnetic waveform or conversion efficiency is modeled. No mains or physical wiring needed.
derivation: Faraday: changing magnetic flux through a coil produces EMF; a stationary magnet gives none.
During charging, V_C=E(1−exp(−t/RC)). Capacitor energy is ½CV_C².
Hand work in this ideal source is C E V_C; the remainder becomes resistor heat.
After shaking, V_C decays exponentially; stored energy supplies the load. Opposing force times drive speed equals input power.
worked: At 2 m/s the representative EMF is 4 V. A capacitor approaches but does not exceed that voltage in this circuit.
challenge: Where does the lamp energy come from after your hand stops? Why is the magnet not a fuel?

observations.sampleNote: Ideal RC charging; magnet speed2 m/s

title: Measure waves with virtual chocolate
materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
question: Are neighbouring hot regions a whole wavelength apart?
encounter: Measure the gap between neighbouring hot regions in the ideal field map. Predict whether doubling that gap gives the wavelength.
procedure: Use the supplied virtual pattern. Enter adjacent hot-region spacing in centimetres and frequency in GHz.
Repeat several spacings and record the resolution. Compare the resulting estimates.
Explain why arbitrary melt spots in a real oven may not be adjacent antinodes. No appliance experiment is required.
explanation: A simple standing wave has neighbouring antinodes half a wavelength apart. Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
limits: One-dimensional ideal standing-wave pattern. A real oven has several cavity modes and nonuniform heating. Virtual food only; never modify an appliance or require a child to handle hot food.
derivation: Adjacent ideal hot regions correspond to adjacent antinodes: d=λ/2.
Therefore λ=2d, not d.
Use c≈fλ=2df, with d in metres and f in hertz.
Repeat spacings and examine resolution; melting alone is not precision metrology.
worked: 6.1 cm and 2.45 GHz give λ=.122 m and speed≈2.989×10⁸ m/s.
challenge: A learner uses c=df. What factor is missing, and what observation justifies it?

title: One light clock, two observers
materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
question: How can the same light have a longer path and the same speed?
encounter: Compare a light pulse between mirrors aboard a carriage with its path in the ground frame. Predict which clock interval is longer.
procedure: Begin at zero relative speed; both frame accounts coincide.
Set speed to0.6c and move the ground-time control through a complete tick.
Compare the same reflection events in both panels. The proper-time clock is aboard the carriage. This is a coordinate account, not delayed camera footage.
explanation: The moving clock has a diagonal light path in the ground frame. Both accounts use the same light speed; the ground-frame tick interval is longer.
limits: Inertial frames, ideal mirrors 1 light-second apart transversely; units c=1. Ground-frame time drives both panels, and ship proper time is t/γ. No acceleration, journey turnaround or gravity. Light travel delay is not time dilation.
derivation: In the ship frame, half a tick takes D/c.
In the ground frame, light travels diagonally: (cΔt)²=D²+(vΔt)² for a half tick.
Solve: Δt=γD/c, where γ=1/√(1−v²/c²).
For the same two mirror events, Δτ=Δt/γ. Each inertial observer may describe the other clock as moving; there is no universal resting frame.
worked: At 0.6c, γ=1.25. A 2 s ship tick takes 2.5 s in the ground frame.
challenge: Is this just waiting longer for light to reach a camera? Explain how the two panels define their times.

title: Many samples, one probability law
materials: Model: nothing. Physical route: coins or two-sided counters on a tray; no radioactive materials.
question: Must exactly half of a small sample remain after one half-life?
encounter: Predict whether five independent samples will follow the same staircase. Compare a small population with a larger one.
procedure: Use the virtual samples or toss a set of coins. Remove heads after each round and toss only the survivors.
Enter round number and survivor count. Repeat the whole experiment with the same initial number.
Compare separate runs with the expectation curve. Do not pool supplied model values with physical observations.
explanation: Half-life is a probability statement. Individual lifetimes vary; an expectation curve describes the ensemble, and small samples fluctuate visibly.
limits: Independent exponential lifetimes with a fixed half-life of 2 model s; five pseudorandom seeded samples. Coins are a probability analogy, not the mechanism of nuclear decay. No radioactive material is used.
derivation: A nucleus has a 50% chance to survive one half-life; previous survival does not make it due.
Expected survivors after time t: N=N₀2^(−t/T_half).
Individual random lifetimes produce staircases; the expected curve is smooth.
For coins, each round is one half-life in the analogy. Compare repeated whole runs, including unusually long survivors.
worked: For 64 initial nuclei, the expected number after 4 s is 16. A particular sample need not contain exactly 16.
challenge: If a nucleus survived ten half-lives, is it now more likely to decay in the next half-life?

title: Build a nucleon; explore the particle families
materials: Paper and pencil; the model works without equipment.
question: Is a proton elementary, or does it have constituents?
encounter: Choose a proton or neutron and add the charges of its three valence quarks. Then explore which particles are matter constituents and which mediate interactions.
procedure: Compare uud and udd. Add charges before revealing the sum.
Select each particle family and read what the model can and cannot explain.
Connect the atom-scale, tracks and parity lessons. Write an evidence-based question that this simple constituent diagram cannot answer.
explanation: Protons and neutrons are composite. Quarks and leptons are elementary matter particles in the Standard Model; interaction bosons and the Higgs have different roles.
limits: Valence-quark bookkeeping, not a picture of quark orbits or a complete proton wavefunction. Additional sea quarks and gluons matter. Gravity is outside the Standard Model; most nucleon mass comes from strong-interaction energy, not simply quark Higgs masses.
derivation: Up quark charge is+⅔e; down is−⅓e. e is the positive elementary charge.
uud totals+1e; udd totals 0. A neutron still contains charged constituents.
Quarks feel the strong interaction; leptons do not. Photon, gluons and W/Z mediate the included interactions.
The Higgs field gives elementary particles mass through their couplings; the Higgs boson discovery was announced 4 July 2012. This does not explain all mass in a proton.
challenge: Why is a neutron neutral without each constituent being neutral? What important physics is missing from three colored circles?

title: Find the right model for a colourful surface
materials: Model and linked experiments: nothing. Optional CD, soap-film image and polarising sunglasses; ordinary reflected light only.
question: Must every rainbow-coloured object act like a prism?
encounter: Compare a prism, a disc with fine tracks, a thin film and a polarising filter. Predict which change in viewing conditions would help tell them apart.
procedure: Choose a surface and make a prediction before opening its linked experiment.
Observe changes with angle, filter rotation or illumination. Record what changed and what stayed fixed.
Return here and explain which model fits. A colour name alone is not an explanation. Use supplied descriptions if the objects are unavailable.
explanation: Different mechanisms can sort or select wavelengths. A grating, a thin film, a prism and a polariser require different accounts.
limits: Schematics and links to the existing calculated optics lessons. Thin-film and grating colours depend on geometry and material; this directory is not a quantitative fit to a particular photographed surface. No laser is required. The filter panel uses Malus’s law for an ideal analyser and initially linearly polarised incident light; it is not a complete model of unpolarised glare.
derivation: A prism disperses wavelengths through wavelength-dependent refraction.
A grating combines contributions from regularly spaced tracks; path differences select bright directions.
A thin film combines reflected paths separated by a thickness; reflection phase matters too.
A polariser selects field orientation. It can change glare without producing a prism rainbow.
worked: Rotating a polariser can reduce a reflected glare patch while a neighbouring matte surface changes less.
challenge: What observation could distinguish a prism rainbow from colours produced by fine tracks?

observations.sampleNote: Malus law; initially linearly polarised light

title: A magnet falls through a conducting tube
materials: Virtual experiment: no equipment. A physical magnet-and-tube demonstration requires adult handling of strong magnets.
question: Can a nonmagnetic metal slow a falling magnet?
encounter: Predict which reaches the bottom first: a magnet in a plastic tube or the same magnet in a conducting tube. Is the conductor attracting it like iron?
procedure: Compare the virtual nonconducting tube with the conducting-tube model. No strong magnets are needed.
Change the drag coefficient and follow the shared time control. Record fall times and compare the two energy accounts.
Explain where gravitational energy goes before the magnet hits the bottom.
explanation: Moving magnetic flux induces currents in the conducting tube. Their magnetic effect resists the motion, transferring energy into warming.
limits: Illustrative low-speed electromagnetic drag F=−bv, mass0.020 kg, one-metre tube. Constant b is a lumped approximation, not a conductivity measurement. No entry/exit field detail. The scene ends at first contact; contact energy is not modeled.
derivation: A conducting tube can carry induced currents even when it is not ferromagnetic.
In this simple model, m dv/dt=mg−bv. At terminal speed, v=mg/b.
For b>0, v(t)=(mg/b)(1−exp(−bt/m)); integrate to get distance.
Before contact, lost gravitational energy equals kinetic energy plus energy transferred into warming.
worked: With no electromagnetic drag, a one-metre fall takes about0.452 s. A conducting tube takes longer in this model.
challenge: Would cutting a lengthwise slot in the conducting tube change the braking? Explain using the current paths.

observations.sampleNote: Illustrative drag model, mass0.020 kg, height1 m

title: Listen to the time between bounces
materials: Supplied intervals need nothing. Optional local audio editor or slow-motion recording for manually identified impact times.
question: What can three impact times tell you about the next bounce?
encounter: Listen for three successive impacts. Predict whether the ratio of the two intervals measures a speed ratio or an energy ratio.
procedure: Use the supplied intervals, or identify three consecutive floor impacts in a local recording using an audio editor or a slow-motion clip. A recording is not uploaded here.
Measure the time between the first two impacts, then the time between the next two. Enter both in seconds. Do not include the initial release-to-first-impact interval.
Repeat the identification and check for echoes or missed impacts. Compare with the video-height route.
explanation: Between two floor impacts, a vertical ball rises and falls. The flight interval is proportional to its launch speed, so the ratio of consecutive intervals estimates restitution.
limits: Manual or supplied impact intervals; no automatic microphone detection. Negligible drag, short contacts, same-height floor, consecutive impacts. Echoes, missed impacts and varying restitution can invalidate the inference.
derivation: Between floor impacts, flight time Δt=2v/g, where v is the upward speed just after a bounce.
Thus the next interval divided by this interval estimates the collision speed ratio e.
The returned mechanical-energy fraction is e², not e.
The peak after an impact is h=g(Δt)²/8; this is not the initial release height.
worked: Intervals1.00 s and0.80 s give e=.80 and energy fraction.64; their peak heights are1.225 m and.784 m.
challenge: If you mistake an echo for the next impact, will the inferred restitution still be trustworthy?
